The code is available at https://github.com/MJonibek/kd-leakage.

papers.title: The Scheduler Is a Hidden Retriever: How Asynchrony Shapes Evidence Acquisition in Search Agents
papers.abstract: Language-model agents increasingly solve complex tasks through parallel reasoning and asynchronous information gathering. Controlled replay across two model families and three benchmarks shows that delivery timing redirects search decisions made before all results arrive, despite identical initial evidence. Acquisition disagreement reaches up to 24 percentage points above same-order repeat variation. This dependence persists after all initial evidence arrives and through a second search, turning temporary differences in what agents have seen into lasting differences in what they acquire. An acquisition-regret bound with a matching construction shows that invariance at a fixed early arrival count can limit the use of evidence already received. We introduce Confluent Evidence Acquisition (CEA), which instead releases local reasoning when each subquestion's evidence is complete and allocates shared search independently of completion order. For a fixed plan and stable conditional response law, we prove joint invariance of decisions, acquisitions, and answers. With question-only plans across three benchmarks, CEA brings acquisition disagreement to within 1.0 percentage point of repeat variation and achieves accuracy comparable to complete-input controls, improving over early commitment by up to 12.6 percentage points. Replacing CEA's fixed allocation with first-ready allocation under contention adds 21.6 percentage points of acquisition disagreement, while local query-target disagreement remains near repeat variation. Timed comparisons show that CEA reaches decisions earlier and responds faster than the same program waiting for all initial evidence.

papers.title: CAST: Cast-Admissible Generative Design and Shape Optimization with Paired Depth Images
papers.abstract: Deep generative design can produce complex geometries, but unconstrained representations may create undercuts that prevent release from a two-part mold. We present CAST, which reformulates three-dimensional shape generation under a selected mold-opening constraint as a two-dimensional image generation problem using paired top and bottom depth images. Each valid depth pair defines one material interval along a selected mold-opening direction, so reconstructions exclude undercuts in that direction by construction. Diffusion models generate candidate shapes in this representation, and a finite element analysis (FEA) guided optimizer refines the same two boundaries. We evaluate diffusion-based generation with limited training data comprising 211 SimJEB bracket designs. On SimJEB brackets, FEA-guided refinement with a volume penalty reduced compliance in 193 of 200 generated candidates. The median reduction across all candidates was 36.8 percent in the optimization FEA model. Reconstruction of existing brackets revealed a mass--stiffness trade-off: filling occluded regions increased material volume and reduced displacement under the evaluated loads. Paired depth images thus connect generative exploration and structural refinement in a shared design space that preserves the selected pull-direction restriction.

papers.title: Answering While You Type: Optimizing Time-to-Answer with Streaming Generation
papers.abstract: Work on efficient large-language-model inference has concentrated almost entirely on reducing the cost of decoding once a request is complete. The quantity a user experiences, however, is the interval between submitting a request and receiving a usable response, and that interval can be shortened without making decoding itself faster. While a request is being composed it is already partially specified, yet conventional deployments begin no computation until submission. We propose and study streaming generation, a decoding regime in which the model begins producing a response from an incomplete request and revises it as the remaining input arrives, so that only a small residue of the answer remains to be computed once the request is submitted. We evaluate the regime on autoregressive and diffusion language models, characterise the conditions under which it reduces user-visible latency, and analyse the mechanism responsible.

papers.title: Robotic Photography System based on Vision-Language-Action Model
papers.abstract: Modern robotic photography requires understanding photographic intent, planning camera motions, and producing aesthetically pleasing images in complex environments. We present RoboPhoto-VLA, a unified Vision-Language-Action framework that jointly models perception, reasoning, and camera control for autonomous robotic photography. RoboPhoto-VLA incorporates PhotoCoT for structured action planning and Aesthetic Direct Preference Optimization (ADPO) to align camera behaviors with human aesthetic preferences. To facilitate training and evaluation, we construct OpenPhotography, a robotic photography dataset with language-guided demonstrations. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that RoboPhoto-VLA produces photographs better aligned with human aesthetic preferences while generalizing effectively to unseen subjects, viewpoints, poses, and complex photographic instructions.

papers.title: Toward Online Robust Zero-Sum Markov Games with Function Approximation
papers.abstract: Online robust zero-sum Markov games pose a coupled operator-learning and game-solving problem: from nominal interaction data, the learner must recover a worst-case minimax Bellman operator while maintaining strategic coverage and controlling stage-game approximation error. Existing robust reinforcement-learning theory does not yet provide such an operator-learning perspective beyond specialized multi-agent settings. We develop an optimistic dual robust Bellman framework that combines dual robust Bellman fitting, optimistic minimax planning, backward-validated confidence sets, and exploiter-mix data collection. Our analysis is organized around the robust Bellman residuals induced by the candidate value class and yields a regret reduction that separates exploration complexity, robust operator-estimation error, stage-game solution error, and misspecification. Under explicit interpretable assumptions, we obtain conditional theorem interfaces for general and projected function approximation, together with closed results in several structured regimes, including tabular, epochwise cross-fit linear, self-normalized pure-online linear / finite-rank kernel, and projected RKHS truncation. Small-scale numerical experiments illustrate robustness calibration, strategic coverage, and the return-gap trade-off predicted by the framework.

papers.title: Learning SOCP Solver Dynamics with Graph Neural Networks
papers.abstract: Second-order cone programs (SOCPs) are a fundamental class of convex optimization problems widely applied across engineering domains. Classical interior-point methods are robust and accurate, but their iterative nature can be costly in real-time or repeated-solve settings. This has motivated learning-based solvers that approximate optimizer solutions with neural networks. Recent work has increasingly studied graph neural networks (GNNs) for linear, quadratic, and second-order cone optimization, leveraging their ability to model sparse relational structure among variables, constraints, and objective functions. Most existing GNN-based solvers compress the optimization process into a single forward pass, predicting the optimizer directly without using the intermediate trajectory produced by classical solvers. We introduce SOCPNet, a recursive GNN framework that uses solver trajectories to learn an iterative SOCP solution procedure. A shared GNN model is applied repeatedly, refining the current iterate at each step and enabling inference for a variable number of iterations. Rather than predicting the solution in a single pass, SOCPNet learns from intermediate iterates to progressively refine its estimates using a trajectory-regularized training procedure. We evaluate SOCPNet on multiple datasets spanning standard SOCP problem classes and show that it consistently reduces the final solution error relative to a SOCP-GNN baseline. Finally, we demonstrate how trained SOCPNet models can be used in a hybrid optimization pipeline by warm-starting a classical interior-point solver, reducing solver iterations without loss of accuracy.

papers.title: Trust Your Targets: Is Target Propagation Block-Diagonal Gauss-Newton?
papers.abstract: Target propagation (TP) is a backpropagation alternative in which local targets carry the global learning signal. Prior works claim that TP performs Gauss-Newton (GN) optimisation on these targets, but the correspondence has only been established under unrealistic assumptions where hitting them exactly is trivial. Practical variants instead descend on a least-squares problem via a single gradient step. In this paper, we rederive TP from a trust region under an implicit, previously unexamined norm, and introduce CGTP (Conjugate Gradient Target Propagation), which uses conjugate gradients to solve the layer-local subproblems in parallel. A single adaptive parameter jointly controls this trust region and a matching bound on the weight update; KFAC emerges exactly as the special case where the per-sample Jacobians are replaced by their batch mean, giving its factored damping a variational grounding. On MNIST and Fashion-MNIST MLPs, CGTP matches the accuracy of ADAM and KFAC while needing orders of magnitude fewer outer iterations than ADAM (about 10x fewer backward-pass-equivalents overall), while remaining stable across depth.

papers.title: Physics-anchored residual quantum neural networks for cloud-cover parameterization
papers.abstract: Compact quantum neural networks have been explored for cloud-cover parameterization, but their predictive value depends on how physical knowledge is incorporated and which classical models provide the reference. We investigate an offline residual formulation that retains a fitted \XR\ cloud-cover estimate and learns a correction to its logit in transformed target space. Using released ICON/DYAMOND-derived data, we compare ten model variants in six- and eight-input settings, with three matched replicates and 10,000 training samples per replicate. All quantum circuits use local Z readout and noiseless exact expectation values. Under a common 30-epoch protocol, residual prediction reduced physical-space test mean squared error relative to direct QNN prediction by 54.3\% and 38.8\% for six-input XYZ and ZZXY circuits, and by 49.2\% and 38.9\% for their eight-input versions. Residual QNNs also outperformed the selected compact residual multilayer perceptron in every paired replicate. A larger, longer-trained Grundner-Q1 adaptation nevertheless achieved lower error: residual Q1 reached mean MSEs of 0.00778 and 0.00791, compared with 0.01124 and 0.01082 for residual XYZ. The results support residual prediction for compact simulated QNNs within the tested budget and establish a clear boundary set by stronger classical references. They do not establish computational quantum advantage or online climate-model skill.

papers.title: A Pitfall in the Evaluation of Gene Perturbation Models
papers.abstract: Gene perturbation models aim to predict transcriptional responses to unseen genetic interventions, but comparisons rely on heterogeneous evaluation metrics and differentially-expressed (DE) gene subsets. We investigate the consequences of these choices using eight methods across six single-gene perturbation datasets under a unified evaluation protocol. Varying the number of top DE genes reveals substantial instability in Precision-based rankings, with the winning method changing $86.7\%$ of the time, while rankings based on the rest of the metrics remain comparatively stable. Investigating this discrepancy exposes that repeating a single predicted expression profile across cell-level rows, a standard practice for many methods, can inflate significance estimates and produce excessively large predicted significant-DE sets. Specifically we found that $67.1\%$ of tested perturbation--gene pairs pass the significance threshold despite some of them having minuscule effects. We derive an inflation factor showing that replicated predictions can amplify the standardized Mann--Whitney statistic even after correction for tied ranks, without adding independent information. This artifact changes Precision mainly as the number of DE genes increases because for smaller cutoffs, most of the genes are already significant due to the effect-based ordering. Taking this pitfall into account in our benchmark comparison, we find that a random forest using Gene Ontology features achieves the best overall results.

papers.title: REFLEX: RNA Ensemble Generation via Flexibility-Calibrated Stochastic Bridge
papers.abstract: RNA molecules often function through multiple experimentally observed conformational states. A central challenge is to capture ensemble diversity without sacrificing structural fidelity: samples may collapse toward averaged representative structures or drift into unsupported conformational regions. We introduce REFLEX (RNA Ensemble generation calibrated by FLEXibility), a sequence-conditioned generator for RNA backbone-frame ensembles based on a heteroscedastic stochastic bridge on SE(3). During training, experimental B-factors calibrate residue-wise bridge widths, exposing each observed conformer through local perturbation neighborhoods with residue-specific scales while keeping constrained regions sharper. A learned flexibility condition guides the bridge-field network to recover target conformer-specific frames from these calibrated noisy states. At inference, REFLEX uses only the input sequence, requiring no MSA-subsampling heuristics. On a multi-conformer RNA benchmark, REFLEX achieves the best precision-recall trade-off for ensemble coverage across evaluation thresholds, while recovery-stress ablations indicate gains in target-frame recovery under stronger perturbations.

papers.title: AudioScorer: Learning Question-Aware Token Relevance for Large Audio Language Models
papers.abstract: Large Audio Language Models (LALMs) reason over speech, environmental sounds, music, and other acoustic information. However, their audio encoders produce dense token sequences that make long-form audio costly to process. Existing audio pruning methods reduce this cost using heuristics such as attention, representation similarity, or temporal sampling, but do not explicitly learn which tokens are most useful for a given question. We propose AudioScorer, a lightweight model that scores audio tokens according to the user question. It is trained by distilling the ranking of audio tokens under the frozen LALM's answer-gradient saliency, together with downstream answer supervision. Compared with other pruning methods, AudioScorer achieves the best or tied-best result at 10% token retention on 7 of 10 semantic and acoustic tasks, including speech recognition, emotion recognition, and audio-scene classification.

papers.title: LOCU: Lowdin-Orthogonalized Constraint Updates for Multi-Constraint Policy Optimization
papers.abstract: We investigate multi-constraint policy optimization in constrained Markov decision processes (CMDPs), where interactions among constraint gradients often yield ill-conditioned update directions, causing numerically fragile steps and unintended cancellation or redundant overlap in constraint corrections. To address this, we propose LOCU, which mitigates numerical instability arising from constraint interactions by applying symmetric Lowdin orthogonalization to the natural gradients of the reward and constraints under the Fisher-Rao metric. Combined with Fisher-geometric screening and near-collinear compression, LOCU yields a compact reduced space in which the trust region becomes a Euclidean ball and constraints are handled symmetrically through a low-dimensional active-set solve. For infeasible iterates, LOCU constructs a Pareto-descent direction which preserves the local feasibility of satisfied constraints within the same reduced formulation. Experiments show that LOCU remains stable under high constraint coupling, narrow feasible regions, and infeasible starts, and generalizes across different cost critic architectures.

papers.title: Structural Context from Audio and Lyric Evidence for Music Structure Analysis Using the New SheetSage-MSA Dataset
papers.abstract: Music structure analysis (MSA) aims to identify functional labels and their boundaries in music. Despite recent progress, three challenges remain. First, fine-grained annotations for MSA are scarce. Second, existing systems often share one encoder between boundary detection and functional labeling despite their different information requirements. Third, most end-to-end systems are audio-only and ignore structural cues from lyrics. To address these issues, we construct SheetSage-MSA, an MSA dataset derived from SheetSage, containing 13,880 cleaned excerpt annotations from 9,010 songs and approximately 82.5 hours of annotated audio. We further propose SCALE (Structural Context from Audio and Lyric Evidence), which uses separate task-specific audio pathways to model local transitions and long-range structural context, and incorporates timestamped lyrics and lyrical recurrence to refine chorus predictions. On the HarmonixSet benchmark, SCALE outperforms the existing state-of-the-art SongFormer by 3.5 and 4.2 percentage points in HR.5F and HR3F, respectively, while improving ACC by 0.9 points. An interactive demo page containing the source code is also available at https://multimodal-music-research-lab.github.io/SCALE/.

papers.title: SEAM: Spectral Embedding Alignment and Merging for Low-Resource TTS
papers.abstract: Expanding the vocabulary of conditional text-to-speech (TTS) models typically requires extensive fine-tuning with paired audio, creating a major bottleneck for low-resource and cross-lingual adaptation. To address this, we introduce SEAM, a zero-audio initialization method that constructs embeddings for unseen tokens from known subtokens. Unlike standard pooling strategies that ignore sequential structure, SEAM applies a spectral filter to preserve temporal phonetic order and uses closed-form ridge regression to align the new embeddings with the pretrained conditioning manifold. Across three languages and two TTS architectures, SEAM approaches or matches baseline performance using up to four times less training data, reducing sample complexity by 75\% compared to random initialization and mean pooling. Our approach provides a lightweight, reproducible, and theoretically grounded solution for vocabulary expansion in low-resource speech synthesis.

papers.title: Beyond Static Leaderboards: Capability-Focused Evaluation with Structural Diversity for Time Series Foundation Models
papers.abstract: Static public benchmarks for time series foundation models (TSFMs) typically have fixed and narrow test distributions. Their repeated reuse encourages benchmark-specific tuning, making reported performance reflect adaptation to the fixed test set rather than genuine forecasting generalization. In addition, a single aggregate score cannot fully characterize model capabilities across distinct temporal structures and input relationships. We propose CaFE (Capability-Focused Evaluation), a refreshable evaluation extension grounded in original benchmark data that enriches static benchmarks with structural diversity and enriches single-score black-box evaluation with multi-dimensional, capability-oriented assessment. CaFE first profiles the original benchmark and defines eight Structural Features (SFs) that characterize its temporal structure. For each SF, it resamples the original data according to its structural support, removes edge-of-distribution samples, and augments the retained samples by varying the SF's salience, producing samples with different structural profiles. After filtering out out-of-distribution samples while preserving diversity, CaFE yields a refreshed evaluation set. TSFMs are then evaluated on this set using both conventional forecast-error metrics and intervention-response metrics, giving each model a per-feature capability profile alongside endpoint accuracy. Experiments on GIFT-Eval and FEV-Mini20 show that CaFE yields stable evaluation results and reveals per-feature strengths and weaknesses that a single aggregate score hides. Moreover, on genuine data filtered by structural condition, models selected by CaFE outperform those chosen by the aggregate leaderboard. CaFE therefore makes model selection conditional on the structural response of interest.

papers.title: RECAP: Reciprocal Sparse Attention and Hierarchical Caching for Efficient Video Diffusion
papers.abstract: Diffusion transformers generate high-quality videos but remain computationally expensive. Sparse attention and temporal caching reduce computation within and across denoising steps, respectively, offering a natural composition. However, predictions produced with sparse attention become sources for temporal reuse, coupling their errors along the sampling trajectory. We observe that improving the accuracy of these sources recovers fidelity without changing the reuse schedule, and that sparsification errors remain directionally aligned across nearby steps, suggesting that correction information can be shared rather than recomputed. These observations motivate RECAP, a training-free method that couples sparse attention with hierarchical caching through reciprocal correction, adaptively coordinated by online error feedback. Cached dense refinement corrects omitted interactions in current sparse estimates, while fresh sparse statistics track input changes and regulate the aging correction. The resulting predictions then renew the sources for whole-step prediction reuse, allowing prediction history to advance between dense refreshes. We evaluate RECAP on multiple video diffusion models against sparse-attention methods, caching methods, and their direct compositions. On HunyuanVideo at 720p 5-second generation, RECAP achieves a 3.05x speedup and outperforms all tested direct compositions in both fidelity and inference speed.

papers.title: Machina Pauliana: A neuro-symbolic approach to the actio pauliana in Dutch insolvency law
papers.abstract: Applying a legal provision frequently requires both structured rule-based reasoning and sensitivity to open-textured terms developed in case law. The actio pauliana of Article 42 of the Dutch Bankruptcy Act (Faillissementswet, Fw), which allows an insolvency practitioner to avoid transactions that prejudice creditors, requires both. We present a neuro-symbolic model of Article 42 Fw. Its symbolic core is written in Catala in a literate style that keeps statute and formalisation aligned and was developed through pair programming, with open-textured terms represented as boolean inputs where neural components couple to the symbolic solver. A neural routine structures a case's natural-language facts into boolean and date inputs. Neural subroutines resolve the open-textured terms through case-based reasoning over Dutch civil judgments, retrieved through a pipeline that filters on the requirement being resolved and expands along the procedural chain of a case. Segmenting and labelling those judgments attains high precision and recall against a manually annotated gold standard of 100 judgments. On ten hand-annotated cases the neuro-symbolic model handles most criteria reasonably but struggles with the knowledge requirement. Retrieval depth shows no clear quantitative effect, although retrieved judgments provide explicit grounding in prior case law.

papers.title: CoRS: Fast Neural Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling via Composite Interval State Reuse
papers.abstract: Neural solvers for the Flexible Job-Shop Scheduling Problem (FJSP) typically refresh graph representations and update feasibility after every operation--machine decision. However, only feasibility must remain exact at every step, whereas graph encoding is substantially more expensive and can potentially be refreshed less frequently. We present CoRS, which decouples them: an interval-level graph representation is reused across multiple sequential decisions, while a stepwise feasibility state is updated after every action. This two-timescale design amortizes graph encoding without parallelizing action generation or relaxing scheduling constraints. CoRS further develops a feasibility-preserving composite-interval decoding scheme with dynamic constraint tracking and boundary state synchronization, which reduces representation refresh frequency while maintaining continuous feasible schedule construction. Furthermore, to alleviate representation staleness caused by interval-level state reuse, CoRS introduces enhanced static features as a compensation mechanism. By providing more comprehensive structural information of the scheduling problem, these features improve the model's perception of overall problem characteristics. Extensive experiments on synthetic and multiple public FJSP benchmarks demonstrate that CoRS significantly reduces inference time while maintaining competitive solution quality, achieving favorable speed-quality trade-offs under tight wall-clock budgets and low-latency scenarios.

papers.title: Shaping the Document, Not the Model: Optimized Suffixes for Context Following
papers.abstract: When a user supplies a document and wants the answer drawn from it, a language model is expected to follow it even when it contradicts its parametric knowledge. Prior work has focused on making the model rely on context by steering activations, contrasting logits during decoding, or instructing it in plain language. We ask whether the document alone, with no instruction written into it and no access to the model at inference time, is enough. We optimize a document suffix by discrete token search, starting from the answer to a single question and extending the objective to a set of passages, to multi-hop questions that follow from the planted fact, and to later turns of a conversation. On counterfactual passages that contradict parametric knowledge of the model, the suffix flips nearly all items the model resists across three instruction-tuned model families, in most settings outperforms the decoding baseline and the strongest instruction we could write, and matches activation steering. Controls show that the suffix largely acts through the passage rather than injecting the answer, and a single suffix per model transfers to unseen passages. Each extended objective carries the effect to its target, so the objective, not only the document, sets how far the effect reaches.

papers.title: Heartbeat Thinking: Speculative Reasoning and Tool Execution While Listening in Realtime Voice Agents
papers.abstract: Tool-using voice agents often leave users waiting after speech ends, even when actionable information arrives earlier in the request. Speculative approaches begin work during speech, but chunk-bounded or interrupt-on-update generation can truncate a tool call before its arguments are complete. This couples computation time to speech updates, limiting useful work completed in advance. We introduce Heartbeat Thinking, which handles updated input through new Thinker invocations while allowing ongoing invocations and dispatched tools to finish. Periodic invocations read the latest partial transcript and a shared record of completed reasoning and tool results. These results help resolve missing arguments and initiate dependent calls, allowing preparation to progress across speech updates. Across SpeechFCEval, FDBench v3, and AudioCRAG, Heartbeat improves aggregate speculative tool coverage or retrieval reuse over a SHANKS-style windowed baseline, with benchmark-dependent effects on final task quality. On FDBench v3, it increases tool coverage by 16 percentage points and reduces mean final-response latency by 36.4\%. The results show that heartbeat thinking paradigm preserving ongoing computation during speech can turn listening time into reusable preparation for faster and more capable voice-agent responses.

papers.title: Towards More Granular Reasoning: Mapping the DSA Transparency Database Taxonomy to Platform Terms and Conditions Using Large Language Models
papers.abstract: Article 24(5) of the Digital Services Act (DSA) requires providers of online platforms to submit every content moderation decision they make, with a corresponding Statement of Reasons (SoR), to the DSA Transparency Database (DSA-TDB). Such decisions are classified against seventeen high-level attribute categories that categorize the primary reason for the moderation decision. Because over 99.8% of statements cite a violation of the provider's own terms and conditions rather than a legal provision, the database is overwhelmingly a record of contractual enforcement using catch-all reporting; however, whether its categories actually describe those contractual rules well has not been examined. In this paper, we map the terms and conditions (T&C) of 31 designated online services against the DSA-TDB's high-level category taxonomy using a few-shot GPT-4.1 classifier over 447 policy documents. The analysis concerns how T&C rules are represented in the taxonomy, not how they are enforced. Two findings emerge. First, high-level category applicability varies sharply by service type: unsafe products account for 17.5% of e-commerce assignments and 0.2% of adult-platform assignments, and negative effects on civic discourse reaches 9.9% within the Meta family but is absent from adult platforms, Booking.com, and Wikipedia. Second, the categories have notable overlap among sub-category specifications, which makes assigning a single high-level category to a decision difficult. We argue that catch-all reporting is plausibly in part a consequence of the DSA-TDB's schema and attribute design, and recommend a schema that is differentiated by service type with more mandatory attributes derived inductively from platform governance language.

papers.title: Rethinking BPE: Merge Selection as Model Selection
papers.abstract: Subword tokenization methods such as Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) are a core component of modern language models; yet, tokenizer capacity remains typically determined by a fixed merge budget, chosen heuristically. Since larger vocabularies increase memory usage and computational cost, selecting compact and effective token inventories is essential for efficient language modeling. We study the optimization of a BPE merge budget as a statistical model selection problem and investigate information-theoretic criteria for \emph{computing optimal merge sets} directly from corpus statistics. To further improve the merge selection in limited data conditions, we augment the BPE training corpora with synthetic texts generated from the original data, providing estimates for the unigram and bigram distributions. Experiments across multiple corpora and downstream tasks show that using a principled vocabulary selection technique reduces model size, with little degradation in performance. We further observe that synthetic data can yield better tokenizers, especially in low-resource settings.

papers.title: Fairness or Fallacy? Mapping the Landscape of AI Bias in Disease Detection
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has several transformative effects on healthcare, like to facilitate clinicians in disease detection and to manage patient care with enhanced precision. Due to the increasing complexity of medical data and the growing volume of diagnostic images, the substantial computational power needed to process such information creates both opportunities and challenges. To accomplish this objective, numerous methodologies have been proposed to integrate AI into disease detection systems. All these methodologies consider different aspects of clinical diagnosis, considering key parameters such as the type of AI model employed, the nature of input data, and the population demographics being analysed. In this paper, we review different state-of-the-art techniques which have been proposed for various areas of disease detection, specifically focusing on bias identification and mitigation. The proposed solutions are distinguished based on the type of input data they utilize, the architecture of model, and type of bias (algorithmic bias, demographic bias, model bias, and deployment bias). The time frame chosen to filter out relevant studies is between 2015 and 2026. Eventually, we review 23 related articles out of 64,389 analyzed from seven different digital libraries. The obtained results guide us to reach a conclusion with respect to state-of-the-art selected studies. Furthermore, these results reveal significant research gaps that can assist researchers in addressing AI-related bias in medical diagnosis. By prioritizing explainability, data diversity, and fairness in algorithmic design, as well as equitable access for affected patient populations, they can utilize available healthcare resources more effectively.

papers.title: LLMs Prompted for Legal Context Refuse More: Overrefusal from Small On-Premises LLMs in Criminal Legal Context
papers.abstract: Confidentiality requirements increasingly push legal professionals toward small, on-device LLMs that keep case data in-house, used for everyday tasks such as summarization, translation, and reformulation. Following standard prompting guidance, a user naturally states their role (``I am a lawyer...''). We show that this innocuous habit has an unexpected cost: such authority framing can make the model selectively refuse legitimate requests, introducing bias through uneven access to assistance. We evaluate four modern small open-weight LLMs on benign legal-domain prompts to measure this over-refusal. Surprisingly, we find that authority-style prefixes (''I am legal counsel working for a national supreme court'', ''I'm a defense lawyer'') systematically increase refusal rates by 2--20x over the no-prefix baseline, while a known role-play jailbreak prefix shows mixed effects, sharply increasing refusals in some models and barely shifting them in others. The finding suggests that small on-prem deployable LLMs are unstable under contextual framings that a real institutional user might naturally introduce, and further investigation is essential to minimize opportunities for bias.

papers.title: OceanTensorCube and ST-MMT: A Multimodal Data and Transformer System for Seven-Day Forecasting of Pyropia Bleaching
papers.abstract: Bleaching of cultured Pyropia (laver) causes losses in Korean seaweed farming. We present a system that forecasts bleaching seven days ahead for farm clusters. OceanTensorCube aligns 32 channels from public marine, meteorological, ocean-model and satellite sources on a 30 m grid, and ST-MMT, a 9.2-million-parameter spatiotemporal transformer with hub-style multi-head cross-attention between variable groups, maps a 14-day input window to a seven-day-ahead bleaching probability. On the validation set, a six-seed ensemble detects every reported positive at a false-alarm rate of at most 3.5%, an upper bound because the report-based labels are positive-unlabeled. A same-date control on separately trained models indicates that the architecture discriminates between clusters when the calendar is held fixed. We also report the system's weaknesses: skill falls steeply as the quarterly nutrient survey ages (ROC-AUC 0.94 at 30 days, 0.53 at 129 days), and a single LSTM on cluster-average series outperforms a single ST-MMT, with only the ensemble leading at the operating point. We describe the labeling procedure, the evaluation protocol and the operational gate that withholds forecasts when inputs are stale. The forecasting service is operated at https://oceantensor.ai.kr.

papers.title: TaQFormer: A Treatment-as-Query Transformer with Data-Fusion for Multidimensional Treatment Modeling in Coupon Allocation
papers.abstract: We study coupon allocation on an online marketplace offering multiple service categories. Issuing coupons requires choosing a vector of category-specific discounts, accounting for both their direct effects and cross-category demand shifts. We present TaQFormer, a treatment-as-query Transformer for this multidimensional treatment setting. Each treatment coordinate is represented as a query token, allowing cross-attention to estimate the response to the full treatment vector. To combine large but policy-biased observational logs with a smaller stream of randomized controlled trial data, we use a two-stage pipeline: observational pretraining learns general outcome patterns, followed by LoRA fine-tuning on RCT data with a request-specific fusion gate. We evaluate the resulting system through the checks required for production, including offline uplift metrics, treatment-parallel serving, latency monitoring, and a 14-day online A/B test. At essentially the same subsidy cost rate, \model increases business value per user by 1.26\% over the production baseline and significantly outperforms both the production baseline and the RCT-only model, while meeting the latency budget. It was subsequently rolled out to all marketplace traffic and has operated at full scale for several months as of October 2026. The deployment illustrates how multidimensional treatment modeling and observational pretraining, combined with adaptation using RCT data, can support effective joint discount decisions in production.

papers.title: GeoEdit: Adversarial De-Evidencing for Silent Geoprivacy Protection via Image Editing
papers.abstract: Recent efforts have demonstrated the strong capabilities of Multimodal Large Reasoning Models (MLRMs) in geographic reasoning. By jointly analyzing subtle visual cues, these models can infer the locations of photos, thus enabling doxing even by non-expert adversaries. Existing defense methods struggle to balance the shareability of photos with effective protection, and often fail to sufficiently disrupt the implicit geo-evidence chains embedded in scene semantics. To this end, we propose GeoEdit, an adversarial de-evidencing framework for silent geoprivacy protection via image editing. Specifically, we apply minimal edits to high-risk evidence anchors in the image, thereby disrupting the underlying spatial reasoning chains while preserving overall scene semantics. We identify these anchors by combining structured knowledge with adversarially discovered geographic cues. To further navigate the large editing action space, we adopt a learnable policy to iteratively refine editing decisions, distilling successful trajectories into transferable natural-language insights for consistent and efficient editing. Evaluated on LifePhotoBench, GeoEdit achieves strong protection against 6 mainstream MLRMs, outperforming visual perturbation baselines by over 0.59 in image fidelity.

papers.title: VEILED-SH: Vulnerability Expression through Indirect Language Evaluation Dataset (Self-Harm)
papers.abstract: AI systems may miss indirect, culturally situated distress or provide support mismatched to the application context. Existing benchmarks do not jointly address cultural variation, application context, and practitioner disagreement. We introduce VEILED-SH, a benchmark and construction methodology for evaluating single-turn responses to indirect expressions of suicide, self-harm, and distress. Its 10,003 prompts span counselor chat, forum posts, platform search, and triage, drawing on Singapore-grounded sources and public datasets. An expert-validated multi-label taxonomy distinguishes intent, communicative function, and response behavior. Six automated profiles, individually calibrated to three peer-support practitioners and three clinicians, retain separate reference policies for proxy-alignment scoring. Evaluating five systems on a coverage-enriched sample reveals variation in proxy alignment across profile-generated reference policies, even for the same system responses.

papers.title: On Counting Graphs for Modal Logic with Counting
papers.abstract: In this paper, we study the theoretical computational complexity of counting trees and graphs that are classified positively by a graph neural networks, or said equivalently that satisfy a given formula of modal logic with counting. We also study convergence.

papers.title: MoveBench: A Rubric-Based Benchmark for Evaluating Large Language Models in Sports and Health Coaching
papers.abstract: Despite rapid advances in large language models (LLMs), their deployment in the sports and health domain remains high-risk due to the absence of domain-specific evaluation benchmarks. Existing general-purpose benchmarks (e.g., MMLU and HELM) primarily assess broad knowledge and reasoning capabilities, but fail to capture critical domain requirements such as exercise safety, physiological appropriateness, personalization, and actionable coaching quality. This gap is particularly concerning in fitness and health applications, where incorrect or unsafe recommendations can lead to physical harm. To address this limitation, we introduce MoveBench, the first comprehensive benchmarking framework specifically designed for evaluating LLMs in sports and health coaching. The proposed benchmark integrates heterogeneous task formats, including multiple-choice questions (MCQs) and open-ended question answering (OpenQA), grounded in real-world user scenarios and paired with structured rubrics emphasizing safety compliance, scientific validity, and training logic. Through large-scale evaluation of 15 diverse LLMs on 809 questions with 5,012 rubric-level criteria, our results reveal substantial performance variability, particularly in safety awareness, structured program design, and personalization capability, highlighting a critical gap between knowing and doing. Our work establishes a foundational evaluation standard for sports and health LLM applications and provides a reproducible framework for advancing safe, reliable, and context-aware AI-driven coaching systems. Open resources are available at https://github.com/SatoSakula/MoveBench.

papers.title: Reading Time Modeling with Pixel-Based Language Models
papers.abstract: Tokenization-free, pixel-based language models (PLMs) have recently been proposed as an alternative to conventional token-based language models (TLMs), typically motivated by practical considerations, e.g., the flexibility to support new languages or vocabularies. Nevertheless, PLMs also have the potential to serve as infrastructure for computational (psycho)linguistics, where tokenization has been a source of bias in estimating information-theoretic values, such as surprisal, and has pushed the bottom-up visual orthographic features outside the scope. In this study, we first integrate PLMs into the modeling of naturalistic human reading and, in particular, examine their use to estimate next-word predictability, which can also integrate orthographic and parafoveal information. Our results demonstrate that next-word prediction difficulty, computed in pixel space, has strong predictive power for gaze duration and word skipping behavior across various languages. In particular, their advantage is complementary to existing token-level surprisal and entropy estimates. Cross-lingual analyses with script variations also clarify their distinctive visual processing biases, facilitating research into how bottom-up visual information is incrementally integrated into expectation-based reading.

papers.title: Conditional information Retrieval for Longitudinal Survey Harmonisation
papers.abstract: Identifying conceptually equivalent questions across different surveys is a challenging information retrieval task where surface-level textual similarity is insufficient. Two questions may be lexically similar yet assess entirely different sociological sub-concepts, or lexically different yet conceptually equivalent. We introduce a conditional information retrieval framework that addresses this by decomposing the task into two steps: concept extraction, which identifies the underlying sociological concept of a survey question using a fine-tuned generative model, and concept-aware retrieval, which augments question representations with the extracted concept as an explicit conditioning signal for finer-grained alignment. To reflect the realistic data scarcity conditions of specialised social science annotation, we use CLOSER as a case study. Our framework consistently outperforms baselines by 2-3 points in both MAP and Recall. We further analyse fine-tuning strategies including SFT, DPO, and dynamic DPO, finding that SFT delivers the most stable gains while dynamic DPO interacts differently with instruction-tuned versus distilled reasoning backbones. Finally, we demonstrate that a model fine-tuned on a general social science thesaurus (ELSST) transfers robustly to task-specific survey data, offering a practical solution under data scarcity.

papers.title: VISAGENT: An Agent-Based End-to-End Voice Interaction System
papers.abstract: Voice-based public services have evolved from manual switchboards to intelligent platforms to meet modern user needs. However, current systems remain constrained by rigid menu-driven interaction, fragmented vertical services, and limited extensibility. To address these issues, we present VISAGENT, an agent-based end-to-end voice interaction system for large-scale public services that integrates end-to-end speech interaction, hierarchical agent routing, a scalable voice-agent marketplace, and user memory support. The system replaces menu-driven workflows with natural speech and dynamically dispatches user requests to either a general conversational model or specialized domain agents via a two-level routing paradigm that achieves sub-second intent-to-agent selection over hundreds of agents. User memory informs preference-aware agent selection and supplies relevant preferences and context to selected agents, supporting personalized task execution and reducing the need for users to repeat previously provided information. A voice-agent registration mechanism converts task agents into conversational entities, enabling dynamic onboarding and ecosystem-level extensibility. We validate VISAGENT through a real-world deployment in China's 114 hotline across multiple service domains. Experimental results demonstrate low-latency full-duplex interaction, robust routing scalability, and competitive speech naturalness. More broadly, this work advocates a shift from isolated voice assistants toward agent-centric conversational infrastructures, providing a general blueprint for building extensible voice-agent systems in public services and beyond.

papers.title: Dynamical Batching: How Class-Cycling Training Shapes the Internal Structure of Neural Networks
papers.abstract: We investigate whether cyclically varying the class composition of training batches can modify both the performance and the internal organization of neural networks. Motivated by nonequilibrium systems, in which cycling between related sub-goals can make switching between their solutions increasingly efficient, we introduce Dynamical Batching (DB), a sampling protocol that periodically emphasizes each class while leaving the loss and the optimizer unchanged, and compare it with Uniform Batching (UB), in which every mini-batch has equal class proportions. In the regime where standard training fails, DB changes the outcome: on a three-arm spiral, a capacity-limited MLP that plateaus far below perfect accuracy under UB fits the training data under DB. Tracking individual weights, we find that under DB the change between class-specialized states is carried by a smaller set of weights than under UB, and that this set is markedly more persistent from cycle to cycle, on every synthetic dataset we test and in a wider network that fits the data under both protocols. This organization is a signature of the protocol rather than a predictor of its benefit: it appears equally where DB leaves accuracy unchanged. On CIFAR-10, the same protocol modestly improves the test accuracy of a channel-narrowed ResNet-10, a standard residual architecture, and of a second capacity-limited convolutional network. These results show that how class emphasis is distributed in time can shape both the solution a network reaches and the internal structure of the network.

papers.title: DeepSEA: A Multilingual Evaluation Benchmark for Southeast Asia
papers.abstract: While language models have demonstrated remarkable capabilities, their performance remains disproportionately skewed towards high-resource languages. This disparity is particularly acute for the 700 million inhabitants of Southeast Asia, where vast linguistic diversity remains under-represented in existing benchmarks, often suffering from limited language coverage or narrow task scopes. To address this, we introduce DeepSEA, a comprehensive benchmark constructed from established datasets through professional human translation into 12 Southeast Asian languages, spanning both high-resource (e.g., Indonesian, Thai, Vietnamese) and low-resource (e.g., Burmese, Khmer, Lao) tiers across five distinct tasks: mathematical reasoning, scientific reasoning, question answering, abstractive summarization, and machine translation. Extensive evaluation of frontier proprietary and open-weights models reveals that while frontier models like Gemini-3.7-Flash maintain robustness across resource tiers, smaller models face severe performance degradation on low-resource languages. Crucially, models perform better in reasoning and summarization when pivoted through English rather than target languages, exposing a critical dependency on English representations, especially for low-resource languages. Beyond these observations, we provide a cross-lingual error analysis and a cross-script tokenizer fertility analysis. We hope these findings shed light on the development of next-generation inclusive multilingual models.

papers.title: Physics-Driven Framework for QoS-Constrained Satellite System with Non-Linear PA Distortion
papers.abstract: This work develops a physics-driven self-supervised graph learning framework that directly optimizes the distortion-aware precoder under nonlinear correlated power amplifier (PA) distortion, without relying on expensive optimizer-generated labels for a user-centric satellite system. We minimize nonlinear PA consumption subject to user quality-of-service (QoS) constraints under PA nonlinearity for a downlink multi-input-single-output (MISO) satellite system. Our pipeline jointly designs the precoder and admission control that minimize nonlinear PA consumed power. In particular, a graph neural network (GNN) for the design of a distortion-aware precoder is optimized end-to-end in a self-supervised manner using a differentiable Itô-Hermite model of the true modified Rapp amplifier model. The precoder output by the GNN is used to initialize a low-complexity distortion-aware signal-to-interference-distortion (SINDR) tracking algorithm that jointly optimizes for power and admission control. Our proposed physics-based pipeline closely tracks a successive convex approximation (SCA) based solution in consumed power performance with the advantage of faster runtime and a wide operating range covered during training.

papers.title: FLMNet: Self-Ensemble Distillation from Masks to Seeds for Single-Tower CTR Prediction
papers.abstract: Click-through rate (CTR) prediction underpins recommender systems and online advertising, where high-dimensional categorical features interact in combinatorially many ways. Several recent CTR models, such as FinalNet and QNN, report higher accuracy when a network also learns from its own averaged predictions, for example by running the same network under different dropout patterns and training each run toward the average. Why this self-distillation helps, and whether its random sampling is needed, remains unclear. This work shows that as the number of dropout patterns grows without bound, the objective reduces exactly to the label loss of the logit-averaged prediction plus a penalty on how much the dropout copies of the network disagree. When dropout does not affect how a network gates its features, this penalty can be approximated in closed form, and FLMNet is designed on this principle and trains without sampling. Networks trained from different seeds disagree in the same form, and distilling several of them into one network recovers part of their ensemble gain. On five benchmarks against seventeen baselines, the resulting models take the top two places in accuracy with a single network at inference, and the gains of the penalty and of distillation, where measurable, largely add up.

papers.title: Reinforcement Learning Controllers for Fusion Scenario Development
papers.abstract: Scenario development, the design of the waveforms that take a tokamak discharge from breakdown to flat-top, is still an iterative, labour-intensive process. Every candidate scenario has to be simulated with a controller in the loop, and the classical shape and current controllers need low-level actuator references. So the process is iterative and includes a number of trial-and-error steps. We propose to replace the per-scenario controller tuning by a single goal-conditioned reinforcement-learning controller trained once, in advance, against a free-boundary equilibrium and transport simulator. A scenario is then specified only by the target waveforms of the physical quantities of interest (plasma current, line-averaged electron density, LCFS shape, x-point positions), and the controller produces the coil-current and fueling commands that realize them. We demonstrate the approach on an EAST plasma-current ramp-up: the controller takes over a small limited plasma, ramps the current and the density, grows the cross-section, forms two x-points and holds a double-null diverted configuration against sampled shape targets for the rest of a 1.2 s episode. The neural network controller is trained using TQC algorithm. On 1024 test scenarios sampled from a low-discrepancy scrambled Sobol sequence in 11-dimensional target space, the controller forms the divertor in 86% of the cases, holds it for more than 0.5 s in 67% and reaches the end of the episode in a diverted state in 58%, with flat-top tracking errors of a few kA in plasma current, $\sim 0.15\times10^{19}$ m$^{-3}$ in density, $\sim 2$ cm in position and $\sim 8$ cm in x-point location; the failures concentrate at the high-current density ($J$) region which is believed to be physically or from engineering perspective not feasible within ohmic mode.

papers.title: Nash-MOPD: Optimizing Task Trade-offs in Multi-Teacher On-Policy Distillation
papers.abstract: Multi-teacher on-policy distillation (MOPD) aggregates the capabilities of multiple domain-expert teachers into a single student model. However, all domains in MOPD share the student's finite budget of optimization steps and rollouts. Fixed uses constant domain sampling ratios based on corpus sizes; by contrast, D$^3$-MOPD adjusts the ratios using the teacher-student reverse-KL divergence and its recent decrease. However, favoring large recent decreases can direct more training toward domains that already improve quickly, while domains that improve more slowly may receive too few examples. To address inflexible allocation and the risk of giving insufficient training to domains that improve more slowly, we propose Nash-MOPD, an adaptive domain scheduler based on a local minimax game using existing reverse-KL statistics. The equilibrium maximizes the smallest predicted proportional reduction under the local model and gives more prompts to domains that need more examples for comparable improvement. Consequently, Nash-MOPD responds to changing learning progress and supports domains that improve more slowly without extra teacher queries or rollouts. At step 100, Nash-MOPD exceeds both baselines' final mathematics and code checkpoint scores on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and reaches Fixed's on Qwen3-8B-Base. Furthermore, it leads eight of nine reported metrics and is best or tied best on all six mathematics and code accuracy metrics, respectively.

papers.title: Optimal Multi-Kernel Combination for Online Multi-Label Classification
papers.abstract: Multi-label classification is particularly challenging in streaming scenarios, where data arrives sequentially. Online kernel methods offer a promising solution. However, prevailing methods rely on a single preselected kernel, making them prone to suboptimal choices since the global data distribution is unknown in advance in online settings. Although the recent method, Online Kernel Selection for Online Multi-label Classification (OKS-OMC), enables data-driven kernel selection, it fails to fully harness the complementary information from multiple kernels and encounters the curse of kernelization. To address these limitations, this paper introduces a novel online multi-kernel combination method for large-scale multi-label classification. First, an efficient and robust online single-kernel multi-label method is designed. Second, learning an optimal convex combination of multiple multi-label kernel classifiers is formalized as a structural risk minimization problem. An improved alternating optimization procedure is developed, in which the combination coefficients are updated by directly minimizing the objective function, while each kernel classifier is updated by minimizing a surrogate upper bound. This procedure decouples the learning of kernel classifiers from combination coefficients, allowing independent classifier updates via our single-kernel method and accelerating convergence to high-quality solutions. Our multi-kernel method is proven to asymptotically converge to the optimal fixed convex combination of the best fixed single-kernel models chosen in hindsight. Ablation studies confirm that our method's components outperform their counterparts in OKS-OMC. Comprehensive evaluations across 11 datasets and seven metrics demonstrate our method's overall superiority over existing online multi-label methods.

papers.title: Variance-Aware Non-Stationary Bandits:All-Budget Regret Bounds and Adaptation Costs
papers.abstract: Low reward variance reduces estimation cost, but does not eliminate monitoring of arms that may improve while unobserved. We refine the variance--variation tradeoff and characterize how both costs depend on supplied variance and variation budgets in bounded, non-stationary multi-armed bandits. Let $A$ be the number of arms, $T$ the horizon, $B$ a bound on consecutive mean variation excluding the initial vector, and $Q$ a bound on the sum of the largest per-round reward variances. For every admissible pair $Q,B$, the minimax expected dynamic regret is, within a single logarithmic factor, \[ \min\{T,\;A+\sqrt{AQ}+(AQBT)^{1/3} +\sqrt{AT}\min\{B,\sqrt B\}\}. \] The deterministic boundary $Q=0$ is characterized without logarithms. For small positive budgets, a safe calibration phase identifies a common interval containing all future means of surviving arms. Clipping observations to a wider interval reduces the cost of restarting a prior hybrid static-regret algorithm; an original-mean analytical reference controls its residuals without charging the variation of clipped means. Balancing clipping bias and monitoring closes the small-budget noisy regime. Fixed oblivious constructions give the matching lower bound. We also quantify adaptation costs: on a disclosed deterministic one-improvement family, a stationary-regret budget has a matching worst-case change-regret frontier, including a finite improvement pulse. This implies an $Ω((T/A)^{1/4})$ loss when one policy competes with all supplied-budget deterministic oracle rates. The budget-free low-noise scheduling problem remains separate.

papers.title: From Retrieval to Recognition:Knowledge-Enhanced Post-training of Time Series Foundation Models for Classification
papers.abstract: Time series foundation models (TSFMs) have achieved notable progress in classification tasks through large-scale pretraining. However, their post-training practice mainly focuses on implicit parameter fine-tuning, where task-relevant information is entangled with abundant irrelevant knowledge in vast parameter spaces. This may hinder TSFMs from precisely activating useful knowledge for downstream classification. To this end, we propose Retrieval-to-Recognition (R2R), a plug-and-play post-training paradigm that adapts pretrained TSFMs to time series classification. Rather than pretraining a new foundation model, R2R improves how existing TSFMs are post-trained: it introduces a decoupled query encoder to extract discriminative patterns and retrieve instance-level numerical knowledge from a constructed knowledge base. The retrieved explicit knowledge is then fused with the TSFM's implicit parametric embeddings, enabling joint knowledge transfer at both the parameter and feature levels. In this way, R2R allows TSFMs to recall task-relevant patterns learned during pretraining, improving the efficiency of knowledge utilization in downstream classification transfer. Experiments on 158 time series datasets show that R2R consistently improves the classification performance of state-of-the-art TSFMs. Ablation and knowledge-enhanced studies further validate the effectiveness of the proposed framework.

papers.title: Applicability and Generalization of Audio Fingerprinting Methods to Speech
papers.abstract: Audio fingerprinting methods identify audio based on its content, even when the content has been possibly corrupted. Despite their applicability and usage in the speech domain, research and advancements in audio fingerprinting traditionally focus on music and are almost exclusively evaluated on music. We provide insights into speech-oriented audio fingerprinting by benchmarking the best performing audio fingerprinting models on speech data while taking into consideration the effects of noise, reverberation, temporal changes, pitch modifications, and lossy compression. Our findings indicate that audio fingerprinting methods based on self-supervised learning outperform classical approaches on speech data, while the performance of these models on speech is inferior compared to the performance that they achieve on music. Results also include an analysis of false positives, showing that fingerprinting methods are more likely to match with an audio of the same speaker rather than an audio of the same text, when mismatches occur.

papers.title: Don't Rewrite the SID Map: Topology Preservation for Generative Retrieval in Dynamic E-Commerce Search
papers.abstract: Generative retrieval assigns each item a discrete semantic identifier (SID) and retrieves items by autoregressively generating SID sequences. In dynamic environments such as e-commerce, new items arrive continuously, requiring periodic updates to the SID-to-Item mapping and model to maintain retrieval timeliness. Each update, however, can invalidate search paths already learned by the retriever, and the quantitative relationship between mapping change and retrieval quality has not been systematically characterized. We study this problem with extensive controlled experiments over 67 days of large-scale e-commerce search logs and obtain three core findings. (1) SID semantic drift causes severe retrieval degradation that may be masked by large beam sizes: mapping updates reduce HitRate by 41.78-62.05% at beam size 1 but only 8.33-10.85% at beam size 1000, as redundant candidate generation conceals the true severity of drift. (2) The fraction of changed SIDs is strictly monotonically related to retrieval quality: as the remapped fraction increases from 0% to 72.75%, HitRate decreases monotonically, dropping up to 42.66% at beam size 1. Full remapping remains substantially worse than the preservation policy under warm-start training, indicating that short-budget continued training alone cannot repair topology disruption. (3) The SID topology-preserving principle makes even the simplest warm-start strategy highly effective: fixing old-item SIDs, inserting new-items, and warm-starting from the previous model improves old-item HitRate by 10% and new-item HitRate by 109%, validated across two non-overlapping update cycles. These findings distill into a concise deployment principle: insert new-items, freeze old-items; warm-start when possible, otherwise freeze; never change SIDs the model has already learned. A three-week online A/B test on TmallAPP shows UCTCVR +0.29% and GMV +1.16%.

papers.title: Declarative Explanations for Graph Neural Networks: A Demonstration
papers.abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have proven effective for graph analytical tasks, yet their "black-box" nature complicates the understanding of their layer-wise behavior and hinders their application to large graphs. We demonstrate SliceGXQ, an end-to-end declarative and interactive system for querying and exploring layer-wise explanations for GNNs over large-scale graphs. In particular, SliceGXQ provides (1) an interactive graphical user interface for dataset, model, and explanation configuration; (2) a lightweight SPARQL-like parser that allows users to specify target nodes, layers, explanation modes, and constraints; and (3) an integrated execution and visualization workflow that invokes SliceGX as its underlying explanation engine. We demonstrate how users can diagnose a misclassified node, identify problematic layers and influential messages, and perform targeted model debugging, together with large-scale graph interpretation and fraud-detection analysis. Our demonstration video and source code are available at https://github.com/jinzhaoqet/SliceGXQ.

papers.title: Learning from a Bandit Learner
papers.abstract: Classical inverse bandit methods typically aim to recover true reward parameters. In contrast, we infer a demonstrator's subjective beliefs, specifically its internal estimates of suboptimality gaps. We consider no-regret demonstrators that follow randomized policies, such as Thompson sampling, and characterize a family of algorithms for which per-step inversion is possible. This enables gap estimates to be recovered directly from the arm-selection distribution. Our analysis identifies an inherent stability-coverage trade-off: inversion becomes ill-conditioned as the demonstrator concentrates its probability mass on a single arm, while the number of informative rounds depends on the rate at which its policy converges. We establish conditions under which inversion is reliable and provide theoretical guarantees on the resulting estimation error. Experiments on simulated data support the analysis and illustrate how these conditions affect gap recovery in practice.

papers.title: Provable Adversarial Detection: Prime Quantization meets Gromov--Wasserstein
papers.abstract: Adversarial vulnerability persists across modern vision architectures from CNNs to vision language models (VLMs), yet existing detection methods rely on heuristics without theoretical guarantees. We address the fundamental question of when adversarial perturbations can be provably detected from a geometric perspective. Our key insight is that adversarial perturbations cannot simultaneously preserve geometric structure across spaces with fundamentally different properties. Accordingly, we construct two such complementary metric spaces. First, we use a standard CNN embedding space $Z$, where adversarial samples exhibit significant displacement patterns. Second, we build a novel prime-quantized space $P$, that absorbs small perturbations through number-theoretic discretization, resulting in minimal displacement, while preserving discriminability. We then leverage the geometric discrepancies across spaces $Z$ and $P$ to detect adversarial samples. To the best of our knowledge, we establish the first rigorous separation theory for adversarial detection, proving that adversarial samples create unavoidable geometric inconsistencies across both spaces. Our framework provides theoretical guarantees including pixel-level absorption bounds, neighborhood diameter concentration, Gromov-Wasserstein (GW) separation theorems, and practical risk control. Extensive experiments validate our theoretical predictions and achieve consistently strong detection performance across a wide range of attack types and model families.

papers.title: Reliable Before Profitable: QuantHarness for Governing Financial Strategy Development with LLM Agents
papers.abstract: LLM agents can turn natural-language financial research requests into executable and backtested strategies, but a successful run may still implement the wrong rule, use information unavailable at decision time, or obscure how repairs and candidate selection changed the strategy. Because these failures arise throughout development, final code and performance metrics alone are insufficient to establish either fidelity to the request or the validity of the development process. We therefore address the reliability of financial strategy development at the trajectory level: the system must control how intermediate outputs become downstream state and preserve the evidence needed to justify the terminal outcome. We introduce QuantHarness, a two-layer agent harness in which a finance-specific Workflow structures specification, data grounding, construction, testing, and review, while Harness Core enforces stage-specific information, action, and commitment boundaries. We also introduce FinRelBench, a benchmark that evaluates strategy-development reliability through execution success, requirement satisfaction, and runtime evidence. QuantHarness achieves the highest Task Success at 90.72\%, compared with 74.23\%--84.54\% for the comparison systems. Controlled stress tests show that its boundaries contain targeted violations, while structured run records improve evidence retrieval and support decision replay under the evaluated protocol.

papers.title: Multilingual Voicemail and Answering Machine Detection via Pretrained Audio Embeddings and Gradient Boosting Machines
papers.abstract: Answering machine detection (AMD) is a fundamental task in telephony that classifies whether an answered call is picked up by a human or a voicemail (machine). Despite its widespread use across cloud communication platforms, existing approaches rely on proprietary systems with undisclosed architectures, or require computationally expensive models that cannot operate in real time. We propose a lightweight AMD system that combines pretrained audio embeddings with gradient boosting machines, trained to prioritize the correct detection of human-answered calls. We evaluate seven models across two datasets: three models that we propose, a proprietary industry model, two prior academic approaches, and a large language model baseline that relies on automatic speech recognition. Furthermore, we release OpenAMD, the first publicly available AMD dataset comprising of more than 500 recordings in 7 languages. Our best model achieves the highest precision across both datasets while maintaining low inference latency. We assess the robustness of models to additive noise and packet loss, and perform tests of statistical significance to discover per-language and per-gender model performance. Finally, we evaluate our model on an out-of-domain task of detecting robocalls, where it achieves 94.34% recall without any additional training, which is comparable to the industry standard.

papers.title: From Code to Playable Systems: CEGame-Bench for Long-Horizon Game Creation Agents
papers.abstract: A game ships when a player can launch it, finish it, and return to a saved world, none of which a successful build guarantees, yet game-creation agents are mostly tested on one engine or on one-prompt browser games. We present CEGame-Bench, the first long-horizon benchmark for complete-game creation across five production engines: Defold, Godot, Roblox Studio, Unity, and Unreal Engine. Agents build each game from an empty project and a design document in runs averaging up to 295 steps and 65M tokens; the document doubles as a contract, and a hidden evaluator accepts a game only by real-input play. Under four scaffolds, agents earn most integration points but usually under half the gameplay points, and their games reach the ending in only 16% of runs, while references built by engineers with coding agents score near the maximum, which places this artifact-to-play gap in the agents. No two engines rank configurations alike (Kendall's tau 0.14-0.62), and the same game usually scores higher on Unity and Unreal Engine, which check more before play. We release Game Completion Boost, an agent skill for requirement-driven playtesting and repair that raises the execution-based score of three models by 14.1-24.3 points.

papers.title: How Robust Are Prognostic Radiomic Features? Comparing Selection Techniques on Pooled Glioblastoma Cohorts
papers.abstract: Radiomic survival studies in glioblastoma report heterogeneous prognostic features, but how much of this stems from the methodology itself is rarely examined. We analysed the association of 463 radiomic, anatomical and clinical features from pre-treatment MRI with overall survival in 705 IDH-wildtype glioblastoma patients from three public cohorts, using three techniques: a log-rank test after median split, univariate Cox regression (both Benjamini-Hochberg corrected) and an XGBoost regressor interpreted with SHAP. The log-rank test selected 99 features, Cox regression 72 and SHAP its top 20; five were selected by all three: age, a peritumoural T2 texture feature, the number of connected peritumoural mask components and two image-level intensity maxima. The two survival tests shared 51 features, about half of the SHAP top 20 were also selected by either test, and where selections overlapped, effect directions agreed. Many selections were PyRadiomics diagnostic descriptors that are not restricted to tumour voxels. Analytical pipeline choices, including ranking method, pre-filtering and descriptor handling, can substantially influence which features appear prognostic.

papers.title: LeakBench: Auditing Reward Hacking through Prediction-Time Leakage in Clinical Modeling Agents
papers.abstract: Autonomous clinical-modeling agents can optimize predictive performance while violating conditions that make a model usable. We introduce LeakBench, an executable, guideline-derived audit suite that tests agent decisions for prediction-time leakage, calibration, site-level evaluation, support awareness, and decision-curve net benefit. LeakBench combines a synthetic task with known failure structure and two real-data settings: MIMIC-IV (430k admissions) and governed multi-hospital inpatient record front-page (MHFP) data. Our primary analysis uses reward hacking descriptively, without attributing intent: an agent selects prediction-time-invalid inputs because they improve its validation reward. A deterministic optimizer and every evaluated unconstrained local-model configuration select a fatal leaking feature. In fully logged September 2026 A/B runs, DeepSeek Flash and GPT-6-astra each leak in 10/10 unconstrained runs and 0/10 runs with an explicit admission-time constraint. This contrast is version-sensitive: a blinded Claude/Fable-5.1 chat run does not leak in either condition, while explicit-constraint violations appear only in a historical August 2026 slice lacking raw trajectories. Replacing AUROC with AUPRC does not remove leakage selection. Renaming or disguising the leaking inputs changes neither selection nor provenance-based detection; a name-based filter fails. A deterministic provenance verifier-in-loop removes the leak, making the LLM repair loop defense-in-depth. Specific verifier feedback clears fatal leakage in a hosted agent, and a three-seed ablation finds principle-only feedback clears decision-level defects, though these mitigation results are limited. LeakBench treats trustworthy clinical prediction as a property of an agent's modeling process, not merely its score; it is an audit testbed with known-failure controls, not yet an expert-validated benchmark.

papers.title: Not All Similarity Is Leakage: Distribution-Aware Identity Leakage Assessment in Synthetic Face Datasets
papers.abstract: Synthetic data provides the means for more ethical and less biased facial recognition. Nonetheless, the limitations of generative models and the conditioning process they rely on pose a risk of identity leakage, resulting in synthetic samples that are overly similar to those seen in a generator's training set, mitigating privacy benefits. In this work, we show that previously proposed approaches are affected by two key limitations: high classifier dependence and a tendency to identify leakage with respect to real datasets that were not used in training. To address these shortcomings, we propose a novel metric called Scaled Overlap (SO), which adapts a non-parametric data-copying test for facial recognition and extends it to the identity level. By leveraging a multi-model setup that compensates for errors in individual classifiers, it provides insights into the true strength of identity leakage. Our analysis identifies leaking datasets (CemiFace, SFace2, IDNet) with the most acute leakage introduced by generative model conditioning in CemiFace, demonstrates that real datasets do not contribute equally to generator training, and shows that the majority of synthetic images are drawn from multiple identities rather than relying on a single identity. Ultimately, our study provides new insights into the quality of synthetic datasets and gives more reliable techniques to help the community ensure the trustworthiness of synthetic data.

papers.title: CUA-Lite: An Open Platform for Computer Use Agents
papers.abstract: Open resources for computer use agents (CUAs) -- environments, datasets, and models -- remain scattered: without a standard, these resources cannot be integrated and scaled; additionally, evaluation, RL, and SFT cannot share one infrastructure. We present CUA-Lite, an open platform for developing CUAs, built around three standardized abstractions: (1) Unified environment interface, under which we integrate 12 benchmarks across desktop, browser, and mobile, plus lightweight VM-free sandboxes that replicate OSWorld's desktop at much lower cost, providing over 30,000 verifiable tasks. (2) Unified supervised data format, into which we convert the major public CUA datasets, from GUI grounding and understanding to full rollouts, and record our fresh rollouts from frontier CUAs on these verifiable environments. (3) Model harnesses shared across evaluation, RL, and SFT, one per model and implemented for 14 model families. Each harness runs its model in these computer environments, producing the rollouts that evaluation and RL consume, or renders stored supervised data into the model's own training format for SFT. We release reference scores across the integrated benchmarks, and show that RL and SFT through the same harness improve open-weight models. We release our dataset, code, and models, and the platform is open to contributions.

papers.title: FinSafeGuard: A Quality-Driven Synthetic Dataset for Financial AI Safety
